definition: Volatility means the tendency to change rapidly, sharply, and unpredictably — swinging in any direction without warning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word volatility. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know volatility should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Analysts warned that election-year volatility in fuel prices could whipsaw the airlines twice in a single quarter.
Fluctuation is milder than volatility: prices fluctuate a few points in any ordinary week, while volatility means swings sharp, fast, and wide enough to make traders flinch.

Upheaval goes further than volatility: a volatile market still swings inside a working system, while upheaval tears the system itself loose — exchanges close, rules change, nothing stands where it stood.

Instability is shakiness in the footing — an unstable ladder, government, or patient is liable to give way. Volatility adds motion: rapid, sharp swings in both directions, which can ride on top of a foundation that never actually fails.

Turbulence is the churn of a rough passage — air, water, or a stormy stretch of history tossing everything caught in it. Volatility is measured in reversals instead: quick, steep swings from one extreme to the other and back.

For two years the vintage-sneaker resale market ran on volatility and nothing else: a pair that traded at ninety dollars on Monday hit four hundred by Friday, fell to one-sixty over a weekend rumor about reissues, then doubled again before the rumor was even disproved.
Sellers set alarms for three a.m.; buyers learned to feel seasick just reading a price chart.
Volatility is the right word because the market's defining trait was the speed and size of its swings — in both directions, over and over.
It was not instability: the shops stayed open, the shoes were real, and the system never once threatened to give way.
The danger was never collapse; it was whiplash.
Volatility is the market page's word for sharp, fast swings in any direction — prices, polls, tempers.
Note what it does not claim: a volatile stock may end the year exactly where it began, because volatility measures the ride, not the destination.
When the danger is weak footing and collapse, reach for instability; when the danger is whiplash, volatility.

Every briefing at the Lake Sorrel ranger station begins with the same warning, and it is not about bears.
Guides call the basin's weather the most changeable in the range, and the logbook backs them up.
One July page records four full reversals in an afternoon: bright sun at noon, a hailstorm by one, sun again at two, and a second squall before three.
Rangers stress that the lake itself is no hazard — the water is calm, the trails are sound, the shoreline stable for decades.
The danger is the weather's volatility: swings so fast and so complete that a kayaker dressed for the morning can be dressed wrong three times before dinner.
